title: Analytica explicatio methodi maximorum et minimorum

deep.reconstruction:
Setting. The functional is J[y] = ∫_0^a Z dx. Z depends on x, y, p = y', q = y'', r = y''' and so on. It also depends on a running integral Φ(x) = ∫_0^x 𝔷(x, y, p, q, …) dx. Write dZ = L dΦ + M dx + N dy + P dp + … and d𝔷 = 𝔐 dx + 𝔑 dy + 𝔓 dp + ….

Previous page. Euler varies J. Integrating ∫ L δΦ dx by parts with V = ∫L dx, normalised so V(a) = 0, turns the nonlocal term into −∫ V δ𝔷 dx. The problem therefore reduces to the ordinary one with modified coefficients N − V𝔑, P − V𝔓, …. The Euler–Lagrange equation is Σ(−1)^k d^k/dx^k (coefficient_k − V·𝔠_k) = 0. Because V(x) = −∫_x^a L dt, the 'indefinite' equation depends on the upper limit a.

This page, Coroll. 3. With both ends fixed (y and its derivatives at 0 and a), any admissible variation of the interior values gives a smaller (maximum) or larger (minimum) value of J. Euler states this as the meaning of the extremal relation; it is really only the first-order stationarity condition.

Coroll. 4. If the end values at x = a are free, the boundary terms must vanish at x = a. These are the natural boundary conditions:
- (P − V𝔓) − d(Q − V𝔔)/dx + d²(R − V𝔑)/dx² − … = 0
- (Q − V𝔔) − d(R − V𝔑)/dx + … = 0
- and so on.

Coroll. 5. A subtlety follows. At x = a we have V = 0, but V' = L, V'' = L', … need not vanish. The derivatives must therefore be expanded generally, writing dV/dx = L, before setting x = a. Only the undifferentiated V terms may be dropped.

Coroll. 6. If the initial values at x = 0 are also free, the same boundary expressions must vanish at x = 0. There V ≠ 0 in general, since V(0) = −∫_0^a L dx. The boundary term VδΦ vanishes at 0 because Φ(0) = 0. These conditions fix the integration constants of the Euler–Lagrange equation.

Problem 3 (begun). Z now depends on two running integrals Φ = ∫𝔷 dx and Φ' = ∫𝔷' dx. The variation δZ = LδΦ + L'δΦ' + Nδy + … is set up. The next page completes it with two adjoint functions V and V', both vanishing at a.

Modern reading. V is (minus) the costate/adjoint variable, i.e. a Lagrange-multiplier function for the auxiliary state equation Φ' = 𝔷 with free terminal value. The condition V(a) = 0 is the adjoint transversality condition, and Coroll. 4 gives the natural boundary conditions.
errors: Coroll. 3 asserts that the relation gives a true maximum or minimum against all variations. Only first-order stationarity has been established; no second-variation or sufficiency argument is given. This is standard for the period.

Coroll. 6 is slightly elliptical. At x = 0 the adjoint V does not vanish, so the boundary expressions keep their full V-terms. Euler only says 'eadem sunt observanda'. It is correct, since δΦ(0) = 0 makes the VδΦ term drop at the lower limit, but this is not spelled out.

ideas.what: Reduction of a functional whose integrand contains a running integral Φ(x) = ∫_0^x 𝔷 dx to an ordinary Euler–Lagrange problem with modified coefficients N − V𝔑, P − V𝔓, …, where V = ∫L dx vanishes at the upper end
ideas.modern_name: adjoint/costate variable (Lagrange multiplier function) for an integro-differential constraint; Euler–Lagrange equation for nonlocal (Volterra-type) functionals
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler, Methodus inveniendi (1744), ch. III, where the same quantity V appears in the geometric method; recast here analytically. Costate interpretation: Lagrange multipliers (Lagrange 1788), Pontryagin et al. 1956–62
ideas.where_published: Methodus inveniendi lineas curvas (E65, 1744), ch. III; E297 itself (Novi Comm. 10)

ideas.what: Natural boundary conditions at a free endpoint, including the higher-order hierarchy for y', y'', …, with modified coefficients
ideas.where_published: E296 Elementa calculi variationum and E297 (both Novi Comm. 10, 1766)

ideas.what: Warning that V(a) = 0 but its derivatives (L, L', …) need not vanish at a, so expressions must be expanded before substitution
ideas.modern_name: careful evaluation of boundary terms containing adjoint derivatives

ideas.what: Extension to several running integrals Φ, Φ', each with its own adjoint V, V'
ideas.where_published: E297, next pages; Methodus inveniendi ch. III

deep.surprise_reason: The adjoint-function treatment of integrands containing indefinite integrals is already in Methodus inveniendi (1744). Its analytic δ-version here is discussed in standard histories (Goldstine, Fraser). The costate analogy is known. Nothing new beyond careful boundary-condition remarks.
transcription_corrections: Coroll. 4: 'determinationi nostrae permittantur' is correct; the second equation's d-term should be d(R − V𝔑)/dx with fraktur 𝔑 (Euler's 'R'), consistent with the image.
Problem 3 statement: 'tantum per quantitates x, y, p, q, r etc. determinentur' — the transcription is fine.
